extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; writers and students of poetry and travel prose
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetry (especially war poetry and lyric pieces) and travel literature, drawn from criticism of Addison's works. Emphasizes truthfulness, choice of models, diction/verse qualities, use of particulars, and completeness of cultural reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manly and rational rejection of fiction in war-poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise the real qualities of military genius (energy, sagacity, military science, firmness of mind) rather than inventing or exaggerating physical exploits as Homeric monsters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: servile imitation of Homeric hyperbole (e.g., Silius Italicus or poets who describe generals doing prodigious single-handed slaughter). Example praise: Addison 'reserved his praise for the qualities which made Marlborough truly great, energy, sagacity, military science... above all, the firmness of that mind'. Scoring note: value verisimilitude and explanatory depiction of strategic qualities over fictionalized brute-heroics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid servile Homeric imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not imitate Homeric manner when describing modern battles or events that have little in common with Homeric warfare; such imitation produces absurdity and nausea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites Silius Italicus and later versifiers who attributed thousands of deaths to a single hero as a detestable fashion. Writers should adapt form and diction to the realities of their subject, not force ancient epic modes onto inappropriate modern subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the particular over the general for rhetorical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular, contemporary, or vividly remembered image often produces a stronger rhetorical or poetic effect than a general or abstract one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the simile 'Such as, of late, o'er pale Britannia pass'd' referring to the November 1703 tempest — the particular historical storm made the simile extraordinarily effective for contemporaries. Scoring note: reward effective, specific images tied to lived or historical particulars rather than generic abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match poetic form to subject and personal gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the poetic form best suited to the subject and to the poet's strengths (e.g., leave heroic couplets to certain masters, blank verse to others, and consider airy songs for lighter material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay suggests Addison 'had left heroic couplets to Pope, and blank verse to Rowe, and had employed himself in writing airy and spirited songs, his reputation as a poet would have stood far higher.' Anti-pattern: clinging to a grandiose form unsuited to one's natural talent or the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness and elasticity of verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines should 'glide' and 'bound' with ease — a pleasing smoothness and an elastic, lively movement in the verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay praises Rosamond for 'the smoothness with which the verses glide, and the elasticity with which they bound.' Scoring guidance: value musical flow, easy cadence, and flexible rhythm appropriate to the poem's mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure and flowing prose style with apt classical allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel prose (and by extension other literary prose) should be written in a pure, flowing style and may make frequent, happy classical quotations and allusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay: Addison's Travels is 'read with pleasure: the style is pure and flowing; the classical quotations and allusions are numerous and happy; and we are now and then charmed by that singularly humane and delicate humour.' Reward clarity, elegance, felicitous classical reference, and gentle humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include modern/local literary and historical references in travel writing
rubrics_metrics.description: A good travel account should address not only classical associations but also the history and literature of the region's modern and vernacular traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of Addison: his Travels 'contains little, or rather no information, respecting the history and literature of modern Italy' and omits figures like Dante, Petrarch, Ariosto, Tasso. Anti-pattern: concentrating almost exclusively on classical sources to the neglect of important modern/local writers and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance models and influences thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose literary models (classical, French, local) consciously; excessive devotion to one tradition can blind a writer to other valuable traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay notes Addison's favourite models were Latin and favourite critics French, which led him to care 'far less' about modern Italian literature. Guidance: avoid unreflective loyalty to a single school; consider wider comparative perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of omissions when aiming for a comprehensive account
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author intends to produce a comprehensive or authoritative account (e.g., of travels or a culture), omissions of relevant material (historical, literary, or descriptive) are legitimate grounds for criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay points out specific omissions in Addison's Travels (no mention of Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio, Machiavelli, etc.). Scoring note: mark down significant lapses of scope or awareness in works advertised as comprehensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tone, charity, and moderation in character depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayal of persons (even rivals or fools) should avoid coarse retaliation; cultivate suavity, moderation, and humane charity in tone and treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay attributes to Addison 'suavity and moderation' and notes 'his zeal was tempered by a regard for truth, humanity, and social decorum' and that he avoided retaliatory outrage. For biographical or satirical writing, reward measured, humane judgment over vindictiveness; anti-pattern: spiteful lampooning that sacrifices dignity.
